title: Coding and testing
subtitle: Testing cannot prove a program correct — but well-chosen tests find most of the bugs, cheaply.

std.title: Coding practice
std.body: Follow a coding standard: meaningful names, small functions, comments that say why, consistent layout, no duplicated logic. Code review catches defects and spreads knowledge. Refactoring improves structure without changing behaviour — safely, only with tests.

levels.title: Levels of testing
levels.body: Unit tests check one function; integration tests check modules together; system tests check the whole against requirements; acceptance tests are run by the customer. The test pyramid says: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few slow end-to-end tests.

bb.title: Black-box techniques
bb.body: Equivalence partitioning: split inputs into classes that should behave alike and test one of each. Boundary value analysis: bugs cluster at edges, so test min, min+1, max−1, max and just outside. A field accepting ages 18–60 has partitions <18, 18–60, >60 and boundaries 17, 18, 19, 59, 60, 61.
bb.steps: Valid range 18–60. Boundary tests (two-value form): below, on, above each end. Test values: 17, 18, 60, 61.

wb.title: White-box and cyclomatic complexity
wb.body: Coverage measures how much code the tests execute: statement, branch, path. Cyclomatic complexity V(G) = E − N + 2 (or decisions + 1) counts independent paths — the minimum number of test cases for basis-path coverage. V(G) above about 10 marks code that should be split.

tdd.title: Test-driven development
tdd.body: Write a failing test (red), write just enough code to pass (green), then clean up (refactor), and repeat. The tests document behaviour and let you change code fearlessly.

dbg.title: Debugging and reliability
dbg.body: Reproduce, isolate (bisect the input or the history), find the cause, fix, add a regression test. Reliability is measured by MTBF; availability = MTBF/(MTBF + MTTR).
